title: S*LM—Intelligence by Division of Labour: A 10-Minute Synthesis
listing_description: A rigorously qualified case for agent systems that allocate language work among compact models, specialists, symbolic engines, deterministic software, larger models, and humans according to contracts and authority.
reader_hook: Suppose the next advance in agentic AI is not one model that does everything, but a runtime that knows which component should do each thing. Enter a research programme built around minimum sufficient generality, explicit contracts, independent checks, and selective escalation.

sections.heading: Replacing scale-first thinking with allocation
paragraphs: S*LM accepts the demonstrated value of scale while rejecting the assumption that one general model should own every operation in an agentic workflow. A useful agent must interpret an underspecified request, preserve prohibitions, resolve entities, retrieve authoritative state, calculate, plan, call tools, validate effects, remember outcomes, and explain what happened. These operations demand different kinds of competence and carry different risks. The book therefore changes the unit of analysis from an isolated model to the complete controlled process that moves language into consequential state changes. Its guiding question is not how small a universal assistant can become, but how much generality each role actually requires. Large models remain appropriate for novelty, broad synthesis, and unfamiliar concepts. Compact or specialized models become plausible where distributions recur and outputs can be validated. Exact computation, state transitions, and policy may belong to symbolic or ordinary software. Consequential authority remains distinct from fluent proposal.

sections.heading: Small, specialized, symbolic—and deliberately heterogeneous
paragraphs: The star in S*LM is a wildcard. A component may be small, specialized, symbolic, or combine these properties; the label describes a system family, not a claim that planners and solvers are language models. Smallness is deployment-relative: it matters when a model crosses into local execution, inexpensive high-volume serving, lower latency, offline use, or proximity to private data. Specialization can concern task, domain, interface, policy, or hardware, each with different validation and maintenance costs. Symbolic structure begins when representations and operations can be inspected independently of next-token probability: schemas, queries, constraints, plans, programs, databases, or proofs. This taxonomy resists easy equations. A domain model is not automatically authoritative. Valid JSON is not faithful intent. A solver proves properties of its encoding, not that the encoding represents the user correctly. Heterogeneity is valuable only when each substrate receives work matching its actual strengths and limitations.

sections.heading: Minimum sufficient generality and progressive compilation
paragraphs: The programme’s design objective is minimum sufficient generality, not minimum parameter count. Every role should declare an input distribution, output contract, failure envelope, authority level, and escalation path before a model is selected. A closed intent set may need only a classifier; flexible schema-bounded arguments may justify a compact generative model; exact search may belong to a solver; unfamiliar synthesis may justify a frontier model. The central research hypothesis is that recurring agent trajectories can be progressively compiled. Early systems use general models heavily to interpret requests and generate examples. As stable subproblems become visible, organizations can convert them into labelled datasets, adapters, validators, deterministic functions, symbolic procedures, and versioned capability packages. This migration is not assumed to work everywhere. Semantic diversity, distribution drift, maintenance cost, translation errors, or weak out-of-distribution detection may prevent specialization from paying. Repetition creates the opportunity; rigorous evaluation decides whether it is real.

sections.heading: The language-to-action stack
paragraphs: Decomposition begins at semantic intake. Requests contain goals, entities, constraints, ambiguity, language variation, and prohibitions whose survival must be tested through the whole workflow rather than at an isolated classification step. Transformations such as translation, summarization, normalization, extraction, and redaction need explicit invariants—especially around negation, modality, quantities, temporal order, exceptions, and uncertainty. Formalization then converts accepted interpretations into schemas, queries, plans, logic, or code, but compiler success must remain separate from semantic fidelity. Planning and tool use should yield governed state transitions, not merely plausible action text. Compact action models are credible where tool surfaces and policies are stable, training data is executable, and abstention works. Workflows own retries, timeouts, compensation, and durable state; policy gates determine which proposed effects are admissible. Evaluation follows the entire trajectory, including partial failure, duplicate actions, recovery, and whether the final state actually satisfies the user’s qualified request.

sections.heading: Memory, routing, recovery, and escalation
paragraphs: A dependable agent does not treat memory as a longer prompt. Working state, factual claims, prior trajectories, and reusable procedures have different origins, lifetimes, authorities, and write rules. Stored objects should preserve provenance, validation state, sensitivity, version, and expiry; candidate memories must not silently become facts. Retrieval must consider authority, recency, dependency, and access policy alongside similarity. Verification likewise produces differentiated warrants: a parser validates syntax, a test covers selected behavior, a solver proves a result under assumptions, and a model judge supplies another probabilistic opinion. Recovery rules distinguish transient failures, invalid arguments, conflicting evidence, policy violations, and irreversible partial actions. Escalation is designed work, not collapse: unresolved evidence and failed checks are packaged for a larger model, specialist, formal method, or human. Routing remains an open problem because cost savings are unsafe if the router cannot identify novel or high-consequence states. Contracts may provide stronger signals than generic preference scores.

sections.heading: Trust and authority belong to the architecture
paragraphs: The book rejects trustworthiness as a personality trained into one courteous model. An agent can sound aligned while reading forbidden data, obeying prompt injection, overwriting valid state, or explaining events inaccurately. Decomposition can improve governance by narrowing roles, separating evidence collection from evaluation, enforcing permissions outside models, and recording causal traces of inputs, tools, versions, decisions, and approvals. It can also make matters worse by multiplying lossy transformations, correlating nominally independent agents, or creating false confidence in formal syntax. Local models can reduce external data exposure but still require access control, retention, encryption, and deletion. Specialized models permit deeper testing but may fail sharply outside their envelope. Symbolic policies enforce exactly what was encoded, including defective policies. Trust must therefore be allocated: a model may recognize intent without authorizing payment; a solver may check constraints without defining them; a human may approve an action while still needing calibrated evidence. No single confidence number captures these differences.

sections.heading: Economics, deployment, and multi-agent discipline
paragraphs: The relevant economic unit is successful, governed work—not tokens, parameters, or one model call. Cheap inference can become expensive through retries, silent errors, human correction, maintenance, or policy incidents. Specialization has fixed costs in data, adaptation, validators, integration, monitoring, and compatibility, so it is most attractive for frequent, stable, measurable roles. Quantization, distillation, adapters, local runtimes, and hardware-aware design can change deployment regimes, but the final artefact must be evaluated on its actual device and contract. Multi-agent systems face the same discipline. Several identical models with theatrical roles do not create independent expertise. Multiple agents earn their coordination cost when they supply genuine parallelism, distinct tools, separate data boundaries, or different verification warrants. Typed artefacts should carry claims, patches, tests, plans, and counterexamples between workers. A well-designed heterogeneous team behaves more like a distributed program than a simulated meeting, and sometimes one model with two tools remains the better system.

sections.heading: Why read the complete book
paragraphs: The complete book supplies the evidence discipline that keeps its architectural proposal from becoming a slogan about small models. It distinguishes established practice, convergent signals, research hypotheses, and conditional outcomes throughout; surveys compact model families, function-calling research, neural-symbolic systems, routing, memory, reliability, security, deployment runtimes, and agent frameworks; and repeatedly states what each result does not prove. Its role taxonomy and appendices make the proposed division of labour concrete, while the research programme specifies domains, experiments, metrics, capability-package contents, and falsification conditions. Readers also gain book-specific qualifications easily lost in a compressed account: semantic translation may dominate solver error, routing may erase portfolio gains, specialization may fail to amortize, and ordinary software may be the best S*LM component. The full work’s value lies in this combination of architectural ambition, operational detail, surveyed evidence, and explicit permission for the thesis to fail.
